extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and academic researchers preparing grant proposals, job applications, email correspondence, and mathematics books
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative standards for writing grant proposals, curricula vitae and job application materials, professional e-mail, and mathematics books aimed at academic mathematicians and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the program prospectus and follow its rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the prospectus for the program to which you are applying. Doing so, you will learn what the program is looking for, what particulars should be itemized in the proposal, what page limits will be enforced, and when the proposal is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn acceptable type fonts, margins, CV length, references length, how many pages should address previous work vs new work, and other formal constraints. "Grant proposal writing is not a free form activity. Get the rules straight before you begin."

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish credibility: can you do and will you do the work?
rubrics_metrics.description: The main issue that is in the air when your grant proposal is being evaluated is your credibility: can you do the work that is being proposed, and will you do the work that is being proposed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show stature, abilities, track record; demonstrate you are already engaged in the proposed activities; make it plausible you are up to the task. Avoid making it sound as though you've already solved the problem or that you are retooling into an unrelated field (e.g., 'I'm tired of finite groups so now I’m going to do symplectic geometry').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not propose mere retooling or learning on the grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, granting agencies will not provide funds to help you to learn something new, or to retool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the project requires new skills, explain why you're already engaged and have a viable program; if learning is essential, justify it carefully but avoid proposals that read as career changes without prior engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate up-to-date knowledge of the literature
rubrics_metrics.description: You must prove that you are up on the relevant field—not just what is in the published literature but what is available in preprint and other tentative form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant reviewers are peers on the cutting edge and will judge you by their standards. Make clear you know recent preprints and current work so referees won't have to hunt to place your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise and make the proposal self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: You will usually have a page limit. You simply cannot go on at length, or have extensive digressions, or have verbose introductions or chatty conclusions. But you must make the proposal as easy to read, and as self-contained, as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage the referee's interest and teach him/her something without forcing library lookups; verbose or boring prose will be penalized. Make each word count given tight page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact the program officer to tailor your proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be afraid to telephone the granting agency to which you are applying and to talk to the program officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many program officers encourage contact; speaking with them helps you tailor the proposal to program goals and avoid wasting time on proposals that are off the wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete self-evaluation and dissemination plans for education proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals in mathematics education and curriculum often require a section on 'self-evaluation' and a section on 'dissemination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid facile statements like 'we’ll see how happy the students are' or 'I’ll go to conferences and talk with my buddies.' Good self-evaluation includes rigorous measures (motivation experts, tracking, exit interviews). Good dissemination can include textbooks, newsletters, web pages, workshops, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect dissemination and impact in research proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-evaluation and dissemination play an implicit role in a research proposal as well. The dissemination aspect of a research proposal is reflected in your publication record, your invitations to speak at conferences or colloquia, and your collaborative activities. NSF proposals now require a section on dissemination and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior record and plans to show likely impact; include dissemination strategies as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish and proofread proposals thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you submit your proposal, run it through a spell-checker. Check and recheck the grammar. Show it to a senior colleague. Proofread it more times than you think could possibly be necessary, and then proofread it once more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposal that appears hastily prepared or sloppy will irritate reviewers. Your proposal should be 'as slick as glass' and a pleasure to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter concision for academic job applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The cover letter should be brief (well under a page); it should identify you, your present position, the type of position you seek, and your areas of interest. No more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overenthusiastic self-praise or extraneous exclamation points. Lead quickly to your strong points; mention major honors or fellowships succinctly if they strengthen your case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble complete application materials and use centralized systems appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a candidate, then you arrange for all your materials (letters of recommendation, Teaching Statement, Research Statement, Vita, cover letter, and so forth) to be uploaded to the mathjobs Web site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: materials in one place, cannot be lost, multiple viewers. Not every school uses mathjobs; seniors may be exempt. For beginners include preprints and AMS standard cover sheet where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit and include strong recommenders with contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying for any job you should approach three or four people ... and ask whether they are willing to write in support of your application. Include their names, business addresses, phone numbers, e-mail addresses, and fax numbers in a section of your Vita called 'References.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer prominent people recognized in your field. For senior positions solicit more letters; in some countries hiring institutions solicit letters themselves—know local norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence of teaching ability when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Some job candidates arrange to have a sample of their teaching evaluations, or passages from their present institution’s Teacher Assessment Book ... included in their dossier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inclusions can lift a dossier and add substance to letters praising teaching. For junior candidates include one or two letters that say something specific and positive about teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the dossier focused and not overlong
rubrics_metrics.description: People on hiring committees these days often must wrestle with 500 job applications in a season. A big, fat dossier will just turn off a weary committee member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave anything important out, but think carefully about what you include; avoid irrelevant items (e.g., long lists of incomplete papers or odd personal trivia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for the job talk and campus visit
rubrics_metrics.description: If you make the 'short list,' then you will likely be invited to give a talk and to meet your potential future colleagues. This is a make-or-break situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress well (seriously, not formally), give a polished, well-prepared talk, and be able to describe your research conversationally to nonexperts in five to ten minutes. Be ready to identify potential collaborators in the department and to discuss teaching topics and curricular issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor industry applications differently from academic ones
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are applying for a job in the private sector ... the application process may be a bit different from the process in an academic setting. A business résumé is different from an academic Vita.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry typically cares less about academic letters and more about relevant skills; consult guides on resumes and cover letters and ask acquaintances who have experienced industry hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vita is a business document—organize and include professionally relevant items
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Vita is a business document. This piece of paper is a précis of your professional life. Think carefully about what you put into it and how you organize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrelevant or humorous personal entries; present honors and key items so they stand out; include references and contact details so the hiring institution knows when the dossier is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and teaching statements: use appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people include a one- or two-page research statement; many include a statement of teaching philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good research statement helps a nonexpert guide the dossier to an appropriate reviewer. If a teaching philosophy is required, write something thoughtful and thought-provoking; otherwise its value is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include complete headers and subject lines in e-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that your e-mail messages go out with a complete header. This header should include a 'From' line, indicating your identity and e-mail address, and a 'To' line ... It is not mandatory, but is highly desirable, for you to include a 'Subject Line' in the header.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Busy recipients receive many messages; a clear subject helps them sort messages and mail clients use subjects to organize mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not strip headers or send anonymous e-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems allow you to strip away all or part of the header of your e-mail message. I urge you not to do this as such an action is unprofessional and rude. Sending anonymous e-mail is no better than sending anonymous hate mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep identifying information; rude to remove headers and harms professional communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give context when replying to e-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: I often receive e-mail messages that say (in toto) 'Yes, I agree with you completely' ... I often cannot tell what such e-mail is about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either include the original message in your reply or include a sentence indicating what you are responding to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign e-mail messages with your full name and contact info
rubrics_metrics.description: Sign your e-mail message with your full name. The best possible 'signature' to an e-mail message is something like this: [full name, department, address, phones, e-mail].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jokey signoffs; set up an automatic signature in your mail client (Gmail, Eudora, Outlook) to include contact details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread important e-mails and use an editor for serious messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread each e-mail message before it goes out. If the message is important then proofread it several times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose important messages in a familiar text editor at home (use spell-checker, dictionary) so you can revise and sleep on them before sending. Upload and send only when satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful: e-mail is immediate and often permanent
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in the preceding discussion is a major liability of e-mail. Too easily can you write something in haste ... and then it is gone. You cannot retrieve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sending hasty heated responses; consider drafting and revising, and sometimes use hard copy or telephone for delicate matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep e-mail messages brief and memolike
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to keep your e-mail messages brief. ... When writing e-mail, you are sending a memo. Thus make it quick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say what you have to say cogently and concisely and then cease; long conversational e-mails waste readers' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask before forwarding and respect requests for discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: People forward e-mail all over the place, with hardly a thought for the consequences. The courteous thing to do is to ask the author before you forward anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor explicit requests to delete or keep messages private; indiscriminate forwarding may be rude or legally problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transmitting delicate matters by e-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic mail is not as secure as other forms of communication. Any superuser on your system can eavesdrop on your e-mail, and computer bandits can break into the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hard copy letters or telephone for the most delicate matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep line length and formatting portability in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: In the early days of e-mail, a user had to be careful of line length: lines longer than 80 characters were often truncated ... careful users still keep lines no longer than 72 characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long lines may be rewrapped by spoolers breaking commands (e.g., TeX commands). Consider UUENCODE or zip attachments for long files and avoid beginning lines with 'From' or 'from' as it will be altered in transit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose and manage e-mail with appropriate software tools
rubrics_metrics.description: It is convenient to use Eudora or Outlook to manage e-mail. These popular software devices will sort your email messages and put them in pre-determined directories on your hard drive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mail clients to automate signatures, sorting, spam filtering; learn and use your editor (PINE, emacs, vi) to compose and proofread effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something original to say when writing a book
rubrics_metrics.description: First, and foremost, you must have something to say. If you are only repeating, or paraphrasing, what has been said before then you are contributing nothing to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the book contributes new insight or organization; avoid writing merely expository rehashes of existing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan the book thoroughly with a detailed outline
rubrics_metrics.description: The best method for writing a book is to immerse yourself thoroughly in the subject. A place to begin is to write a detailed outline of the book. Begin by writing chapter headings. Then fill in some section headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the outline mentally, jot ideas as they occur, and let the outline evolve; immerse in each chapter and keep notes for other chapters to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for learners: perform a reverse evolution to the learner's perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember, as you write, that you are taking material that you have thoroughly digested ... and are presenting it to your readers—many of whom are tyros. Thus you must perform a reverse evolution to put yourself in the shoes of the learner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain motivation and foundations clearly; avoid skipping steps that novices need; organize exposition to guide newcomers through the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong organization and place lemmas/definitions where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep in mind that organization is a powerful tool. ... do not state lemmas parenthetically. ... Most of the process of developing a book consists of attending to details like making sure that all your lemmas and definitions are in place before you need them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'love letters to oneself' with parenthetical proofs; insert lemmas in the main flow and add connecting material so readers are not forced to hunt for prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for long revision and rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to turn this random sequence of meditations into a publishable book, one that people will read, then some hard work lies ahead. You must go through the MS line by line, detail by detail, attending to context, syntax, logic, motivation, and many other details as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread repeatedly, rewrite sections or chapters as needed, and accept that the revision process is hard and tedious but essential to produce a readable book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing: write major books after tenure if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: My advice is not to consider writing a book until you have tenure and are established somewhere. The task is just too time consuming, and is often not construed as a positive contribution toward the tenure decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junior faculty should prioritize research papers for tenure; consider writing books when you have the time and security to devote years to the project.
